title: To Spot AI, You've Gotta Know Stuff
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a viral explainer on how to detect ChatGPT-written text, Stuart argues that spotting AI-generated content is fundamentally a knowledge problem, not a technology-detection problem. His key example is a fabricated cocktail recipe that reads as plausible unless the reader already knows enough about classic cocktails to recognize the fabrication, meaning without background knowledge a reader has no inclination to even fact-check. He draws the classroom implication directly: since AI can generate inaccurate text at scale, students need a knowledge-rich curriculum more than ever, not less, so they have the background knowledge required to catch errors. He frames his own teaching, built around argument, reading, writing, speaking, and listening tied to substantive content, as already aligned with what a ChatGPT-saturated world demands, even though he doesn't consider his methods innovative.
points: Stuart's core claim is that detecting AI-generated inaccuracy is a knowledge problem: readers without domain knowledge have no inclination to fact-check plausible-sounding fabricated content.

His cocktail-recipe example makes the mechanism concrete: a fabricated recipe for a nonexistent drink reads as legitimate to anyone lacking classic-cocktail knowledge, which is the general pattern for any AI-generated text in an unfamiliar domain.

The practical response he commits to is doubling down on a knowledge-rich curriculum paired with frequent argument, reading, writing, speaking, and listening, rather than adopting new AI-specific tools or detection strategies.
quotes: In order to spot the tells in the AI generated texts, you have to know the content area. In one example, they ask the machine to create a recipe for a classic cocktail that doesn't exist, and the machine does so.

Unless you already know quite a bit about classic cocktails, you really don't have a shot at detecting that the whole recipe is made up. You wouldn't even have the inclination to fact check the text; it wouldn't raise any flags.
What this means practically in my classroom is that I need to keep giving my students a feast of knowledge in all of my courses.

In order to think critically about a text's accuracy on the Internet, my students have got to know at least a little bit about a lot of things. It's been true forever; it's just more important now that inaccurate texts can be so rapidly generated with the new technology.
My classes have never been what I'd call innovative or ground-breaking. But they've apparently been on the right track to preparing students to live in a ChatGPT world.
